content: Nettle refers to a group of 30 to 45 species of flowering plants belonging to the genus Urtica in the family Urticaceae. These plants are distributed globally, with a preference for temperate regions. Most nettles are herbaceous perennials, though some are annuals, and a few are shrubby in nature. The most well-known species is the stinging nettle (Urtica dioica), which is native to Europe, North Africa, Asia, and North America. Other species within the genus share similar characteristics and medicinal properties, particularly the presence of stinging hairs. Historically, many species names within the genus Urtica have been reclassified, with approximately 100 species described in older literature now recognized as synonyms of Urtica dioica. Some of these taxa are still acknowledged as subspecies. Most species in the genus possess stinging hairs, which contain compounds such as formic acid, serotonin, and histamine. However, studies on Urtica thunbergiana suggest that oxalic acid and tartaric acid may play a role in the stinging mechanism for that species. The stings of certain nettles, such as Urtica ferox (commonly known as ongaonga or tree nettle in New Zealand), can be highly toxic and have been known to cause fatalities in animals and humans. The exact nature of the toxins secreted by nettles remains uncertain. Species of Nettle The genus Urtica includes various species with distinct natural ranges: Urtica angustifolia: Found in China, Japan, and Korea. Urtica dioica: Commonly known as stinging nettle, native to Europe, Asia, and North America. Urtica ferox: Known as ongaonga or tree nettle, native to New Zealand, with highly toxic stings. Urtica urens: Known as dwarf nettle or annual nettle, found in Europe and North America. Additional species are distributed across regions such as the Himalayas, Mediterranean, Australia, and the Americas. Other Plants Called Nettles Some plants outside the genus Urtica are also referred to as nettles, though they are unrelated. Examples include: Wood nettle (Laportea canadensis), found in eastern North America. False nettle (Boehmeria cylindrica), which does not sting and is found in the United States. Other unrelated plants with nettle in their name include dead-nettle (Lamium spp.), Carolina horsenettle (Solanum carolinense), and spurge-nettle (Cnidoscolus stimulosus). Ecological Role Nettles serve as an essential food source for the larvae of several butterfly species, such as the Peacock Butterfly and Small Tortoiseshell. They are also consumed by the larvae of various moths, including Angle Shades and Buff Ermine. The roots of nettles are sometimes eaten by the larvae of the Ghost Moth (Hepialus humuli). Uses Culinary The young tops of nettles are commonly used as a cooked green vegetable. Some cooks discard the first boiling water to remove stinging compounds, while others cook them directly. Nettles are available in some farmers' markets and natural food stores. Tea Fresh or dried nettle leaves can be used to make tea, and commercial nettle tea bags are widely available. Medical Nettles are believed to have galactagogue properties and have been shown to act as a diuretic in patients with congestive heart failure. The practice of urtication, or deliberately applying stinging nettles to the skin, has been used as a folk remedy for rheumatism to provide temporary pain relief. Nettle extracts are used to treat conditions such as arthritis, anemia, hay fever, kidney problems, and pain. Nettle root extracts have been extensively studied for their efficacy in alleviating symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Certain nettle extracts, containing 3,4-divanillyltetrahydrofuran, are used by bodybuilders to increase free testosterone levels by inhibiting sex-hormone-binding globulin. Fresh nettles, particularly Urtica dioica, are used in folk medicine to stop bleeding due to their high vitamin K content. However, dried nettles lose their vitamin K and are instead used as a blood thinner. Other Uses Paper: Nettle stems are used in small-scale papermaking. Textiles: Nettle fibers have been used in textiles, though this is more experimental than widespread. Unlike cotton, nettles grow easily without pesticides, but their fibers are coarser. Nettles were also used as a dye in the medieval period. Safety While fresh nettle leaves can cause painful stings and acute urticaria, these effects are rarely serious, except in the case of highly toxic species like Urtica ferox. Most nettle species are safe and can be consumed as vegetables after steaming to neutralize the stingers. Nettles can be harvested safely by wearing gloves or by firmly grasping the plant to crush the stingers before they penetrate the skin. Traditional remedies for nettle stings include rubbing the affected area with the crushed leaf of the dock plant (Rumex obtusifolius), which often grows near nettles. Other remedies include using plantain leaves, mud, or fern spores, though their efficacy is disputed. Nettle stingers can also be removed from the skin by wiping with a chamois or the inside of a leather glove. Popular Culture The Bottle Inn in Marshwood, Dorset, England, hosts an annual World Stinging Nettle Eating Championship. Competitors consume raw nettle leaves, with records held by Jo Carter (34 feet of nettles) and Simon Sleigh (74 feet of nettles in an hour). The phrase grasp the nettle is an old saying that means to confront a difficult situation without hesitation.
